Revisiting the broken symmetry phase of solid hydrogen: A neural network variational Monte Carlo study

Shengdu Chai Affiliation: Interdisciplinary Center for Theoretical Physics and Information Sciences (ICTPIS), Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, China Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai 200232, China    Chen Lin Affiliation: Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford, Oxford OX1 3PJ, United Kingdom    Xinyang Dong Affiliation: Beijing National Laboratory for Condensed Matter Physics and Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China    Yuqiang Li Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai 200232, China    Wanli Ouyang Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai 200232, China Affiliation: Department of Information Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR HKG, China    Lei Wang Affiliation: Beijing National Laboratory for Condensed Matter Physics and Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China    X. October 5, 2026
Abstract

The crystal structure of high-pressure solid hydrogen remains a fundamental open problem. Although the research frontier has mostly shifted toward ultra-high pressure phases above 400 GPa, we show that even the broken symmetry phase observed around 130 GPa requires revisiting due to its intricate coupling of electronic and nuclear degrees of freedom. Here, we develop a first principle quantum Monte Carlo framework based on a deep neural network wave function that treats both electrons and nuclei quantum mechanically within the constant pressure ensemble. Our calculations reveal an unreported ground-state structure candidate for the broken symmetry phase with C​m​c​mCmcm space group symmetry, and we test its stability up to 96 atoms. The predicted structure quantitatively matches the experimental equation of state and gives the closest x-ray diffraction peak-position match among the tested candidates. Furthermore, our group-theoretical analysis provides a symmetry-counting compatibility check between the C​m​c​mCmcm structure and existing Raman and infrared spectroscopic data. Crucially, static density functional theory calculation reveals the C​m​c​mCmcm structure as a dynamically unstable saddle point on the Born-Oppenheimer potential energy surface, demonstrating that a full quantum many-body treatment of the problem is necessary. These results shed new light on the phase diagram of high-pressure hydrogen and call for further experimental verifications.

I Introduction

Understanding the behavior of hydrogen under extreme pressure remains a grand challenge with profound implications [38, 80, 37, 114, 7], ranging from planetary interiors to the pursuit of the metallic, high-temperature superconducting state. Determining the precise structure is fundamental to these goals, as structure dictates the physical properties. Although decades of experimental effort have revealed a rich phase diagram, the detailed structures of high-pressure hydrogen remain largely unsettled. To date, only the structure of low-pressure Phase I is firmly confirmed by experiment as a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice of freely rotating H2\mathrm{H}_{2} molecules [40, 76, 42]. With increasing pressure, the system transitions into a broken symmetry phase characterized by the emergence of long-range orientational order. Early spectroscopic observations established this transition in para-H2, D2, and HD [69, 101, 86]. While recent frontiers have advanced toward the ultra-high pressure regime (>>400 GPa) in pursuit of metallic hydrogen, the detailed structures of the broken symmetry phase are less settled than commonly assumed and require revisiting.

Despite tremendous progress in experimental techniques [40, 76, 42, 72, 5, 34, 35, 33, 44, 45, 68, 69, 79, 43, 51, 52, 6, 32, 71], it is still difficult to unambiguously determine the structure of solid hydrogen under extreme conditions. The extreme pressure conditions and the small, fragile samples restrict feasible probes to low-power optical techniques, such as Raman and infrared (IR) spectroscopy [72, 5, 34, 35, 33, 44, 45, 68, 69, 79, 43]. Moreover, the inherently weak x-ray diffraction (XRD) signals of hydrogen [51, 52, 6, 32, 71] further hinder direct structural identification, making it difficult to discern the signatures of the high-pressure phases.

In light of these experimental difficulties, first principles calculations have proposed several candidate structures for broken symmetry phase, including P​21/c​-​8P2_{1}/c\text{-}8, P​21/c​-​24P2_{1}/c\text{-}24, P​c​a​21Pca2_{1}, C​m​c​21Cmc2_{1}, P​63/mP6_{3}/m, etc. [56, 87, 55, 105, 53, 117, 97, 116, 96, 84, 64, 10, 9, 26, 118, 41, 59], and others even suggested that broken symmetry phase to be a “quantum fluxional solid” [13, 31]. However, these predictions have been inconclusive due to the inherent limitations of standard computational frameworks rooted in the Born-Oppenheimer (BO) approximation and the inadequate treatment of electronic correlations. Static Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations [14, 83, 85, 88, 106] neglect the zero-point energy (ZPE) of protons, a contribution comparable to the cohesive energy in hydrogen, often leading to erroneous stability rankings. While ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) [4, 14, 57] introduces thermal effects, it typically treats nuclei as classical particles, thereby missing critical nuclear quantum effects (NQEs) [78], such as tunneling and zero-point motion. Consequently, classical AIMD cannot intrinsically capture the distinct phase behaviors of isotopes. More advanced methods like path-integral molecular dynamics [14, 92] or path-integral quantum Monte Carlo  [14, 24, 54, 107] rigorously incorporate NQEs and recover isotope effects; however, they rely on an underlying potential energy surface generated by DFT, thus inheriting the systematic errors of approximate exchange-correlation functionals.

Crucially, the contribution of lattice anharmonicity, often neglected or treated insufficiently, is pivotal in determining the structural stability of solid hydrogen [11, 81]. Previous studies have shown that anharmonic correction is “small but significant” and impacts molecular and atomic phases oppositely, significantly shifting predicted phase boundaries [11]. Even state-of-the-art approaches designed to capture these effects, such as the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation (SSCHA) [81], remain constrained by the BO approximation and the assumption of a Gaussian nuclear density matrix. To accurately describe the phase diagram, it is therefore essential to transcend these limitations by employing a framework that supports an intrinsically non-Gaussian nuclear wave function, provides a highly accurate description of electronic correlations, and treats electrons and nuclei on an equal quantum footing to recover nonadiabatic effects.

Neural network based variational Monte Carlo calculation (NNVMC), pioneered by [16] and in particular Ref. [95] for ab initio simulations, has emerged as a powerful way to solve quantum many-body problems accurately and reliably [47, 99]. To date, there have been applications to a broad set of physical and chemical problems, including molecules [39, 95, 46, 94, 28, 60] and solid-state materials [62], moiré systems [63, 75], homogeneous electron gases [17, 93, 104, 110, 30, 58], excitons [74], superfluids [70], high-pressure hydrogen [115, 25, 66], fractional quantum Hall states [100, 108, 29, 3], and topological insulators [61]. Collectively, these studies establish neural-network quantum states as a versatile and systematically improvable framework for first-principle quantum many-body computation.

Building on this progress, we develop a beyond-Born-Oppenheimer real-space neural network framework for enthalpy extremization to investigate solid hydrogen structures. By extending the NNVMC method to the constant pressure (NPT) ensemble [67], our framework simultaneously optimizes the crystal geometry and the full quantum many-body wave function for both electrons and nuclei [111]. Akin to the approach demonstrated in Refs. [66, 67], our framework employs a highly flexible, non-Gaussian representation of the nuclear wave function, thereby treating NQEs and electronic correlations on an equal footing without relying on the BO approximation under NPT ensemble.

In this paper, we apply this methodology to provide new insights into the long-standing issue of the broken symmetry phase of solid hydrogen. Our simulations identify a candidate orthorhombic structure with C​m​c​mCmcm space group symmetry. This candidate is compatible with available experimental observations and gives the closest XRD peak-position match among the tested candidates after uniform volume rescaling. Furthermore, symmetry analysis shows that its allowed vibrational modes are compatible with the spectroscopic signatures observed in Raman and IR experiments.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section II introduces the computational framework and the neural network ansatz; Section III presents the main results, including benchmark results and the newly identified C​m​c​mCmcm structure with its experimental signatures, and demonstrates through static DFT analysis the importance of a fully quantum many-body treatment of the problem; Section IV concludes with a discussion of the implications for the high-pressure hydrogen phase diagram and future directions.

II Methods

We solve the ground state of the full Schrödinger equation for a system of NN hydrogen atoms in a periodic simulation cell with constant pressure. The Hamiltonian is

H^=−12∑i=1N∇𝐫i2−12​M∑I=1N∇𝐑I2+V(𝐫,𝐑),\hat{H}=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\nabla_{\mathbf{r}_{i}}^{2}-\frac{1}{2M}\sum_{I=1}^{N}\nabla_{\mathbf{R}_{I}}^{2}+V(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R}), (1)

where 𝐑={𝐑I}\mathbf{R}=\{\mathbf{R}_{I}\} and 𝐫={𝐫i}\mathbf{r}=\{\mathbf{r}_{i}\} denote the proton and electron positions, respectively. The first two terms denote the electron and proton kinetic energy, respectively. The last term represents the Coulomb interaction, calculated with the Ewald summation technique. We adopt atomic units (ℏ=e=me=1\hbar=e=m_{e}=1), consequently, energies are expressed in Hartree, lengths in Bohr, and the proton mass is set to M=1836M=1836. The overall framework is illustrated in Fig. 1.

II.1 Wave function ansatz

Building a physically valid and expressive wave function is central to the success of the NNVMC framework. We parametrize the ground state wave function as a product of two components

Ψ⁡(𝐫,𝐑)=χ⁡(𝐑)​φ​(𝐫,𝐑),\Psi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R})\;=\;\chi(\mathbf{R})\,\varphi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R}), (2)

where we denote χ⁡(𝐑)\chi(\mathbf{R}) as the nuclear wave function and φ⁡(𝐫,𝐑)\varphi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R}) as the electronic wave function. Note that Equation (2) is different from the Born-Huang expansion [15] in which φ⁡(𝐫,𝐑)\varphi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R}) is treated as electronic eigenstates given nuclear positions. On the other hand, we do not deem φ⁡(𝐫,𝐑)\varphi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R}) to be normalized with respect to the electron coordinates either. Hence, such an ansatz is not the same as the exact factorization ansatz [2, 50]. Equation (2) is just a convenient factorization for the ground state wave function of the electron-nuclei coupled system in Eq. (1), designed to capture the coupled electron-nuclear quantum dynamics without the BO approximation.

We discuss the symmetry requirement of the wave functions and their neural network parametrizations in the following. φ⁡(𝐫,𝐑)\varphi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R}) must be antisymmetric under exchange of electrons and obey periodic boundary conditions (PBCs). χ⁡(𝐑)\chi(\mathbf{R}) must obey PBCs as well, while nuclear exchange symmetry is neglected based on nuclear localization in the molecular broken symmetry phase and prior QMC results showing negligible proton antisymmetrization in a rotationally ordered molecular phase at comparable pressures [18]. Exchange between localized sites is a tunneling process suppressed by the small overlap between permutation sectors [20, 21], so we expect its contribution to the static structural observables and relative enthalpies considered here to be small. We also note that while nuclear spin statistics (para- vs ortho-hydrogen) are energetically crucial for the rotationally disordered Phase I [102, 103], they become secondary in the broken symmetry phases focused on here, where hindered molecular rotations diminish the impact of specific spin configurations. Thus, the spin statistics are also neglected.

To rigorously enforce translational invariance under PBCs, all network inputs are constructed from periodic descriptors. We encode particle relative positions using sine and cosine of fractional coordinates [17], and construct single- and two-particle features 𝐡α​β1\mathbf{h}_{\alpha\beta}^{1}, where α,β\alpha,\beta denote any pair of particles (electron-electron, nucleus-nucleus, or electron-nucleus). The superscript denotes that it is the input feature of the first layer of the neural network.

The explicit, flexible parametrization of the nuclear wave function χ⁡(𝐑)\chi(\mathbf{R}) is a central feature of our ansatz. The nuclear log-amplitude ln⁡χ⁡(𝐑)\ln\chi(\mathbf{R}) is constructed from ion-ion features 𝐡I,J1\mathbf{h}_{I,J}^{1} processed by a deep residual network. We employ a ReZero scheme [12], which introduces a trainable scaling parameter initialized to zero. This design allows the model to start from a physically meaningful periodic distance metric and progressively learn many-body corrections dI​Jenvd_{IJ}^{\text{env}}, thereby capturing anharmonicity in the nuclear wave function. The final log-probability is a sum of squared deviations from learned equilibrium distances bI​Jb_{IJ} with weight σI​J\sigma_{IJ} as follows:

lnχ(𝐑)=−∑I​JσI​J2(dI​Jenv−bI​J)2\ln\chi(\mathbf{R})=-\sum_{IJ}\sigma_{IJ}^{2}(d_{IJ}^{\text{env}}-b_{IJ})^{2} (3)

.

The electronic wave function is developed based on DeepSolid [62], where antisymmetry is enforced through the product of spin-resolved Slater determinants,

φ⁡(𝐫,𝐑)=det[ϕ↑]​det[ϕ↓].\varphi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R})\;=\;\det[\phi^{\uparrow}]\;\det[\phi^{\downarrow}]. (4)

. Single-particle orbitals ϕiα​(𝐫j,𝐫≠j)\phi_{i}^{\alpha}(\mathbf{r}_{j};\mathbf{r}_{\neq j}) are constructed from residual networks acting on electron-ion features 𝐡i,I1\mathbf{h}_{i,I}^{1} and electron-electron features 𝐡i,j1\mathbf{h}_{i,j}^{1}, mixing single- and two-body embeddings across layers to encode higher-order correlations.

Although our implementation follows the overall architecture of DeepSolid, we introduce two key modifications to the original framework to enhance training stability. First, we utilize the sine and cosine periodic embedding [17], discussed previously, replacing the Jastrow factor-based embedding proposed in Ref. [113] to ensure smoother feature representation. Second, we simplify the electron-features construction process. While the original DeepSolid constructs single-electron features based on the primitive cell, we found this approach led to training instability in hydrogen systems. We, therefore, bypass the primitive cell construction entirely and operate directly within the simulation cell.

II.2 Constant-pressure optimization

In the NPT ensemble, the loss function is the enthalpy:

G=⟨Ψ|G^|Ψ⟩=∫d​𝐫​𝑑𝐑​|Ψ⁡(𝐫,𝐑)|2​Gloc​(𝐫,𝐑),G\;=\;\langle\Psi|\hat{G}|\Psi\rangle\;=\;\int\!d\mathbf{r}\,d\mathbf{R}\;|\Psi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R})|^{2}\,G_{\text{loc}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R}), (5)

where G^=H^+Pext​Ω\hat{G}=\hat{H}+P_{\text{ext}}\Omega, PextP_{\text{ext}} is the external pressure, and Ω\Omega is the cell volume; Gloc​(𝐫,𝐑)=Ψ−1​(𝐫,𝐑)​G^​Ψ​(𝐫,𝐑)G_{\text{loc}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R})=\Psi^{-1}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R})\hat{G}\Psi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R}) is the local enthalpy. As shown in Ref. [67], the structure of the wave function allows the enthalpy gradient,

∇ΘG=2​𝔼​[(Gloc−𝔼⁡[Gloc])​∇Θ​ln⁡|ΨΘ|]+𝔼⁡[∇ΘGloc],\nabla_{\Theta}G=2\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(G_{\text{loc}}-\mathbb{E}[G_{\text{loc}}]\right)\nabla_{\Theta}\ln|\Psi_{\Theta}|\right]+\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{\Theta}G_{\text{loc}}], (6)

to be decomposed into two distinct contributions. Here, Θ\Theta collectively denotes the neural network parameters θ\theta and the lattice parameters LL. When optimizing θ\theta at fixed LL, only the first term contributes; conversely, when optimizing LL at fixed θ\theta, only the second term contributes.

However, direct evaluation of the second term, 𝔼⁡[∇ΘGloc]\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{\Theta}G_{\text{loc}}], is computationally expensive. In practice, we avoid computing this costly term explicitly and instead optimize LL via a stochastic simulated annealing procedure, as described below.

At each step, a trial lattice deformation L→L′L\to L^{\prime} is proposed, and the corresponding enthalpy G′G^{\prime} is then evaluated. The move is accepted with the Metropolis acceptance probability min(1,e−ΔG/τ)\min(1,e^{-\Delta G/\tau}), where Δ​G=G′−G\Delta G=G^{\prime}-G and τ\tau is the fictitious temperature, which is used to avoid the risk of trapping in shallow local minima. The fictitious temperature is decreased according to the Lundy-Mees schedule [73], τ⁡(t)=τ01+β​t\tau(t)=\frac{\tau_{0}}{1+\beta t}, ensuring ergodicity at early stages and convergence toward low-enthalpy configurations as the annealing progresses. Here, τ0\tau_{0} is the initial temperature and β\beta is the cooling rate.

A subtle point is that the enthalpies GG and G′G^{\prime} computed in VMC contain intrinsic statistical noise. Using these noisy estimates directly in the Metropolis violates detailed balance. Although the penalty methods can be used to restore exact Boltzmann distribution in the presence of noise [19], our goal is not to generate an NPT equilibrium distribution but to locate the minimum-enthalpy structure without evaluating high-order derivatives. In this optimization context, strict detailed balance is unnecessary, and the noise can even be beneficial (see Fig. S1 and the related discussion in the Supplemental Material (SM) [1]).

II.3 Sampling

To evaluate the loss function and its gradient with respect to the neural network parameters θ\theta, we sample electron and nuclear configurations from p⁡(𝐫,𝐑)=|Ψ⁡(𝐫,𝐑)|2p(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R})=|\Psi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R})|^{2}. A naive one-shot Metropolis update in the joint electron-nuclear space is inefficient and often exhibits low acceptance rates for nuclear moves due to the vast disparity in energy scales between electrons and nuclei. We, therefore, employ a Gibbs block sampler: in each sweep, we (i) sample electronic coordinates 𝐫\mathbf{r} from p⁡(𝐫|𝐑)p(\mathbf{r}|\mathbf{R}) with fixed nuclei, followed by (ii) sample nuclear coordinates 𝐑\mathbf{R} from p⁡(𝐑|𝐫)p(\mathbf{R}|\mathbf{r}) with fixed electrons. Each conditional update uses Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, with adaptive step sizes to maintain target acceptance.

III Results

We first present benchmark calculations of hydrogen with dynamic protons and then move on to the candidate C​m​c​mCmcm structure for the broken symmetry phase of hydrogen. We will analyze its experimental signatures, as well as its stability in more conventional DFT calculations with the BO approximation. These analyses place our computational discovery in context and highlight the importance of a fully quantum treatment of both electrons and nuclei.

III.1 Benchmarks

VMC/DMC has long been a cornerstone method for investigating the phase diagram of dense hydrogen [18, 90, 91, 112, 48, 8, 98, 9, 49]. Given the extensive body of literature available for validation, we first benchmark our method against established VMC/DMC results. Calculations were performed for systems of 54 hydrogen atoms arranged in a BCC lattice with fixed volume at rs=1.31r_{s}=1.31.

Reference data for Slater-Jastrow wave functions using LDA-DFT orbitals (SJ-LDA) and backflow plane-wave orbitals (BF-PW) were taken from Ref. [49], while neural quantum state (NQS) energies were obtained from Ref. [66]. A detailed comparison is presented in Table 1.

Our energies are consistently lower than those of all reference methods, including both traditional and neural quantum state approaches, while maintaining comparable energy variances. This indicates that our ansatz offers enhanced expressivity for the solid hydrogen ground state.

III.2 The C​m​c​mCmcm candidate structure

Having validated our framework, we applied it to investigate the structure of solid hydrogen at 130 GPa—corresponding to the experimental pressure range of broken symmetry phase. NPT simulations were performed on a system comprising 64 protons and 64 electrons. We began by optimizing the most promising candidate, P​21/cP2_{1}/c [59], whose optimization was initiated at an external pressure of Pext=10P_{\text{ext}}=10 GPa, and then gradually increased the pressure to 130 GPa. We found that the structure converged to an orthorhombic structure with C​m​c​mCmcm space-group symmetry, both at Pext=95P_{\text{ext}}=95 GPa and Pext=130P_{\text{ext}}=130 GPa.

To assess the robustness of this result, we performed independent optimizations starting from several structurally distinct configurations, including P​c​a​21Pca2_{1}, P​63/mP6_{3}/m, and P​63/m​m​cP6_{3}/mmc (with aligned molecules), as well as the identified C​m​c​mCmcm structure. These calculations yielded two consistent outcomes among the tested initial structures. First, among the tested initial structures, relaxations starting from both C​m​c​mCmcm and P​c​a​21Pca2_{1} converged to the lowest enthalpies, which were significantly lower—by at least 4 mHa per atom—than those of the P​63/m​m​cP6_{3}/mmc and P​63/mP6_{3}/m phases at 130 GPa. Second, the optimization initialized from P​c​a​21Pca2_{1} not only matched the final enthalpy of the C​m​c​mCmcm structure but also evolved into the C​m​c​mCmcm symmetry, differing only slightly in lattice aspect ratios. Similarly, calculations initialized directly in C​m​c​mCmcm remained stable. Finally, a separate optimization with 96 atoms starting from the C​m​c​mCmcm structure was carried to examine the stability of this structure with respect to system size, and the C​m​c​mCmcm lattice remains stable upon scaling. The convergence from multiple unrelated initial configurations suggests that the orthorhombic C​m​c​mCmcm lattice appears to be the enthalpy minimum within our calculation framework. To extract the equilibrium structure from the optimized configurations, we align the first atom in each batch after training.

Structurally, the discovered orthorhombic C​m​c​mCmcm phase contains 8 H2\mathrm{H}_{2} molecules per primitive unit cell (16 molecules in the conventional cell), as illustrated in Fig. 2. The 32 hydrogen atoms fully occupy the four 8​g8g Wyckoff positions. Notably, this proposed structure can be viewed as a distortion of the hcp structure found in Phase I, consistent with the indirect reconstructive mechanism discussed in previous works [109, 6]. Furthermore, the predicted structural parameters are consistent with experimental measurements. At 130 GPa, our calculated equilibrium volume is 2.063 Å3/atom, within 4.3% of the experimental value (2.156 Å3/atom) reported by Ji et al. [51]. This comparison provides a lattice-metric compatibility check for the C​m​c​mCmcm candidate.

Beyond the lattice symmetry, a defining feature of the identified C​m​c​mCmcm structure is the orientational order of H2\mathrm{H}_{2} molecules. Unlike in Phase I, where the molecules undergo nearly free rotation, the broken symmetry phase exhibits distinct orientational ordering that breaks the high symmetry of the hcp lattice. To quantify this ordering, we computed the joint angular distribution g⁡(θ,ϕ)g(\theta,\phi) by accumulating statistics across the sampled configurations. For each molecule, the orientation is characterized by the polar angle θ\theta and the azimuthal angle ϕ\phi as shown in Fig. 3. The resulting histogram was normalized to yield the probability density. As shown in Fig. 3, the molecules adopt a layered configuration, lying approximately within the a​bab plane. This orientational order naturally explains why the observed c/a=1.586c/a=1.586 in the room-temperature experiment [51] is slightly smaller than the ideal close-packed value of 1.63. A low-temperature measurement at 100 K also reports a similarly reduced axial ratio [6]. Further analysis shows that rotational motion is largely suppressed, while librations persist within the a​cac plane, confined to an angular range of approximately 60∘<θ<120∘60^{\circ}<\theta<120^{\circ}.

To obtain a gauge-invariant measure of electron-nuclear coupling, we evaluate the nuclear kinetic energy in the exact-factorization (EF) gauge [2, 50]. Normalizing the conditional electronic state at each nuclear configuration gives Knon​-​BOEF/KBOEF≈3.7%K_{\rm non\mbox{-}BO}^{\rm EF}/K_{\rm BO}^{\rm EF}\approx 3.7\%. This ratio measures the nuclear-coordinate dependence of the normalized conditional electronic state within the optimized full wave function.

III.3 Experimental signatures

III.3.1 X-ray diffraction

We compare the simulated XRD peak positions of the candidate structures with experiment. As shown in Fig. 4, after the same uniform volume rescaling, C​m​c​mCmcm gives the closest peak-position match among the tested candidates: the forward and reverse RMS errors are 0.1248 and 0.0036 Å for all selected peaks and 0.0039 and 0.0036 Å within the 1.35–1.65 Å window. For C​m​c​mCmcm, Fig. 4 shows both the static and coherent quantum-density-corrected profiles. Although the third peak is relatively weak, internal-coordinate refinement and the coherent-density correction described in the SM [1] slightly enhanced the intensities. Notably, simulated patterns for other proposed candidate structures, such as P​21/c​-​8P2_{1}/c\text{-}8, P​21/c​-​24P2_{1}/c\text{-}24, P​c​a​21Pca2_{1}, and P​63/mP6_{3}/m, exhibit subtle discrepancies compared to the experimental results. In all cases, the volume is scaled to the experimental volume at the same pressure. Current experimental precision [51, 6] is not yet sufficient to unambiguously distinguish several theoretical structures. Nevertheless, together with the NNVMC structural search, this peak-position agreement supports the C​m​c​mCmcm structure.

III.3.2 Vibrational spectroscopy

Vibrational spectroscopy provides a symmetry-counting compatibility check against experiment. Experimentally, the transition from Phase I to Phase II is marked by the appearance of new, broadened vibron features in both Raman and IR spectra, absent in the high-symmetry Phase I, indicating a lowering of lattice symmetry.

We performed a group-theoretical analysis of the vibrational modes for the C​m​c​mCmcm structure to evaluate its spectroscopic characteristics as reference. As summarized in Table 2, this symmetry admits four IR-active and four Raman-active vibrons. Although the theoretical mode count exceeds current experimental observations, the C​m​c​mCmcm symmetry remains compatible with the data, as the experimentally observed features can be interpreted as a subset of the theoretically allowed active modes. This interpretation follows the symmetry-counting comparison previously used for candidate structures of solid deuterium [23]. Because the present all-particle NNVMC method does not directly compute Raman or IR frequencies or intensities, the comparison is restricted to symmetry-allowed mode counting.

The analysis of the lattice phonon modes presents a greater challenge due to limited experimental data in the low-frequency region. As shown in Table 2, the C​m​c​mCmcm structure allows for a rich spectrum of phonon modes. However, no IR phonon modes have been reported in the literature to our knowledge. Similarly, the Raman phonon features are elusive; while earlier work reported a single peak [43], subsequent studies observed that this phonon mode becomes extremely weak [45]. The absence of these theoretical peaks in current data may be attributable to weak signal intensities [116] or peak overlapping characteristic of high-pressure hydrogen experiments, rather than an exclusion of the C​m​c​mCmcm symmetry.

III.4 Stability analysis with static DFT calculations

To understand why the C​m​c​mCmcm structure identified in our calculation was not found in previous DFT-based searches, we performed static DFT calculations using the PBE functional. We conducted variable-cell relaxations (vc-relax) on the C​m​c​mCmcm structure alongside other competitive candidates (P​21/c​-​8P2_{1}/c\text{-}8, P​c​a​21Pca2_{1}, P​63/mP6_{3}/m with unit cells containing 64 atoms, and P​21/c​-​24P2_{1}/c\text{-}24 with 48 atoms). Convergence was strictly verified with Monkhorst-Pack 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point meshes up to 8×8×88\times 8\times 8, ensuring that finite-size errors do not affect our conclusions.

Our static DFT results reveal a significant discrepancy with the NNVMC C​m​c​mCmcm result. Across all tested structures, the relaxed space groups remained unchanged during the vc-relax. Apart from C​m​c​mCmcm, all other candidates exhibit very similar final enthalpies per atom at a given 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point mesh. In contrast to our calculation, the static enthalpy of C​m​c​mCmcm is not the global minimum, it lies approximately 1.11.1 mHa/atom higher than P​c​a​21Pca2_{1}. To further assess the dynamical stability, we computed the phonon spectrum. While other candidates are dynamically stable, the relaxed C​m​c​mCmcm structure exhibits negative (imaginary) frequencies at the Γ\Gamma point. This shows that, on the classical BO surface, the C​m​c​mCmcm lattice is a saddle point rather than a stable minimum.

The fact that C​m​c​mCmcm is a saddle point with higher static enthalpy explains its absence in conventional DFT searches. There are several possibilities for such discrepancy as the static DFT calculation involves multiple approximations that we have relaxed in our many-body calculation. First, there are DFT functional errors [10]. Second, it is well known that strong NQEs, including ZPE, lattice anharmonicity, and even beyond BO effects, may overturn classical structural predictions. A detailed assessment is beyond the scope of the present paper. In the following, we speculate on the effects of lattice anharmonicities and beyond BO contributions in stabilizing the discovered C​m​c​mCmcm phase.

First, NQEs such as ZPE and anharmonicity play a critical role. Although the static enthalpy of C​m​c​mCmcm is higher than that of P​c​a​21Pca2_{1}, the difference is small (∼1.1\sim 1.1 mHa/atom). Once NQEs are considered, the energetic ordering can be reversed. The ZPE of solid hydrogen at this pressure is estimated to be around 1010 mHa/atom based on harmonic phonon calculations [36]. Therefore, even a moderate estimate that different competing structures differ by 10%10\% in their ZPE is comparable to the ∼1\sim 1 mHa/atom difference between the static-lattice enthalpy of C​m​c​mCmcm and P​c​a​21Pca2_{1} structures.

Second, our framework explicitly captures non-BO effects. As detailed in Sec. III.2, the EF-gauge non-BO contribution to the kinetic energy in the C​m​c​mCmcm phase is approximately 0.22 mHa/atom. Although smaller than the ZPE scale, this term may also contribute to the relative structural stability.

Taken together, these results demonstrate that C​m​c​mCmcm is not stable at the static-lattice level within the PBE functional. Instead, its emergence as the enthalpy-minimizing structure in our framework is driven by strong NQEs, including anharmonicity and non-BO effects. This physical picture is consistent with a large body of recent work on hydrogen-rich systems. Errea et al. [27] shows that quantum fluctuations reshape the BO landscape of LaH10, collapsing multiple classical minima into a single high-symmetry phase; and Monserrat et al. [82] demonstrates how anharmonic and quantum effects stabilize otherwise classically unstable high-pressure hydrogen phases. Similarly, our findings also suggest that strong protonic quantum motion may effectively lift the saddle point on the BO surface, transforming it into a minimum on the full quantum energy landscape.

These observations not only explain why previous DFT-based searches missed the C​m​c​mCmcm structure but also highlight the importance of a fully anharmonic and beyond BO description, such as that provided by our method, for correctly determining the phase diagram of dense solid hydrogen.

IV Discussion and Conclusion

The present work revisits one of the longest-standing problems in high-pressure physics—the structural nature of the broken symmetry phase of solid hydrogen. By employing NNVMC framework, which treats electrons and nuclei on an equal footing and directly minimizes enthalpy in the NPT ensemble, we identify an orthorhombic molecular lattice with C​m​c​mCmcm symmetry as the lowest-enthalpy structure in our NNVMC search at 130 GPa. Agreement with the equation of state, the closest XRD peak-position match, and Raman and infrared symmetry compatibility provide three complementary consistency checks for this candidate. Taken together, these results indicate that C​m​c​mCmcm is a potentially competitive candidate for the broken symmetry phase and motivate targeted experimental tests.

An intriguing question is whether the structural transition of the H2\mathrm{H}_{2} hcp structure coincides with the orientational ordering H2\mathrm{H}_{2} molecules. Our analysis suggests that these may be two distinct symmetry breaking transitions. As noted in Ref. [109], the C​m​c​mCmcm symmetry is a maximal subgroup of the Phase I P​63/m​m​cP6_{3}/mmc space group. In the model proposed by Toledano et al., H atoms in Phase I partially occupy the 4​f4f and 12​k12k sites, reflecting the orientational disorder of freely rotating molecules. They proposed that compression induces a transition to a partially ordered C​m​c​mCmcm phase, where fractional occupancy persists (e.g., half-filled 8​f8f and 16​h16h sites), leading to orientational degeneracy and potential topological frustration that could drive an incommensurate modulation.

In contrast, our calculations suggest that the broken symmetry phase is fully ordered, characterized by full occupancy of the 8​g8g Wyckoff positions of the C​m​c​mCmcm space group. The subgroup pathway inferred from our calculations differs from that of Ref. [109]. To link our C​m​c​mCmcm structure to Phase I, we consider a restricted P​63/m​m​cP6_{3}/mmc model where molecules are confined to the a​bab plane (corresponding to partially occupied 6​h6h sites, derived from 12​k12k with z=1/4z=1/4 and the 4​f4f sites are vacated). Under the group-subgroup reduction P​63/m​m​c→C​m​c​mP6_{3}/mmc\rightarrow Cmcm, these partially occupied 6​h6h sites split into the fully occupied 8​g8g positions of the C​m​c​mCmcm structure. Consequently, the resulting phase is free of orientational degeneracy, eliminating the mechanism previously hypothesized to drive incommensurate distortion. Furthermore, unlike many previously proposed candidate structures where molecular centers of mass (COM) retain the hcp lattice positions of Phase I, the COMs in our discovered C​m​c​mCmcm structure exhibit a more complex structure. While the COMs no longer form a simple hcp lattice, the structure can be fundamentally viewed as a distortion of hcp. This symmetry analysis hints at a possible two-step transformation sequence involving an intermediate state that retains P​63/m​m​cP6_{3}/mmc lattice symmetry but lacks free rotation. Further investigation into the coupling between lattice symmetry breaking and orientational ordering is warranted.

On the methodological front, similar to the beyond BO neural wave function approach in Ref. [66], we have developed a general first principle framework for predicting ground states of quantum materials beyond BO approximation within NPT ensemble. The necessity of such an approach is underscored by our stability analysis in Sec. III.4, which reveals that the C​m​c​mCmcm structure is a saddle point on the static PES. It is stabilized only by strong nuclear quantum effects—specifically, the interplay of zero-point motion and nonadiabatic coupling. By treating variable cell parameters as variational degrees of freedom and minimizing the enthalpy of a coupled electron-nuclear wave function, our calculations capture these critical stabilizing mechanisms that standard DFT methods inherently miss. Consequently, the optimal crystal structure emerges naturally as an intrinsic property of the many-body quantum ground state. Scalable to systems with hundreds of quantum particles, this approach provides a versatile tool for investigating systems where quantum fluctuations reshape the energy landscape, making it particularly well suited for exploring higher-pressure hydrogen phases, high-TcT_{c} hydrides, and other light-element materials under extreme conditions.

Localization and prior molecular QMC results indicate that the proton-exchange correction neglected here is small for the static observables considered. The present calculation targets the low-temperature BSP/Phase II regime. Extending direct NNVMC comparisons to A-phase/Phase III structures is an important direction for future work.

In conclusion, our full quantum many-body calculations identify orthorhombic C​m​c​mCmcm as a potentially competitive candidate for the broken symmetry phase within the structures examined. This finding sheds new light on a long-standing problem in high-pressure physics, showing consistency with available structural, spectroscopic, and thermodynamic observations, and motivates further theoretical and experimental assessment. Beyond identifying this candidate, the present work explores a general computational framework for predicting quantum materials under finite pressure, treating electronic and nuclear degrees of freedom on an equal footing. Crucially, our results show that a full nonadiabatic quantum treatment, capturing anharmonicity and beyond BO effects, plays an important role in describing the phase diagram of dense hydrogen. These results motivate further experimental tests of C​m​c​mCmcm in the broken symmetry phase.

I Neural Network Wavefunction

To satisfy the PBCs required by the simulation cell, we map Cartesian coordinates to periodic descriptors via fractional coordinates [17]. Let 𝐫i​j=𝐫i−𝐫j\mathbf{r}_{ij}=\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j} be a relative displacement vector. We decompose this vector into the lattice basis {𝐚k}\{\mathbf{a}_{k}\} as 𝐫i​j=∑k=13ωi​j,k​𝐚k\mathbf{r}_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{3}\omega_{ij,k}\mathbf{a}_{k}. The periodic distance is computed using the lattice metric tensor Sk​l=𝐚k⋅𝐚lS_{kl}=\mathbf{a}_{k}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{a}_{l} as:

d(𝐫)=[(1−cosωk)Sk​l(1−cosωl)+sinωkSk​lsinωl]1/2.d(\mathbf{r})\;=\;\Big[(1-\cos\omega_{k})S_{kl}(1-\cos\omega_{l})+\sin\omega_{k}\,S_{kl}\sin\omega_{l}\Big]^{1/2}. (S1)

The input feature vectors 𝐡α​β1\mathbf{h}_{\alpha\beta}^{1} for the first neural network layer are constructed by concatenating the periodic embedding of relative positions with this distance metric:

𝐡α​β1={∑ksin⁡(ωα​βk)​𝐚k,∑kcos⁡(ωα​βk)​𝐚k,d⁡(ωα​β)},\mathbf{h}_{\alpha\beta}^{1}\;=\;\Big\{\sum_{k}\sin(\omega_{\alpha\beta}^{k})\mathbf{a}_{k},\;\sum_{k}\cos(\omega_{\alpha\beta}^{k})\mathbf{a}_{k},\;d(\omega_{\alpha\beta})\Big\}, (S2)

where α,β\alpha,\beta denote any pair of particles (electron–electron, nucleus–nucleus, or electron–nucleus).

The pseudocode for the nuclear wavefunction and electron wavefunction is given in section I and section I, respectively. As for the sampling algorithm, the two-stage Gibbs sampler is summarized in section I, with the original one-shot Metropolis scheme provided for reference in section I

II Enthalpy operator and coordinate map

Rather than treating lattice parameters as variational degrees of freedom in Ψ\Psi, we incorporate them into the enthalpy operator and sample in unit-scaled (fractional) coordinates [67]. We define the set of all real-space particle coordinates as 𝒳={𝐫i}∪{𝐑I}\mathcal{X}=\{\mathbf{r}_{i}\}\cup\{\mathbf{R}_{I}\} and the corresponding set of fractional coordinates as 𝒮={𝐬i}∪{𝐒I}\mathcal{S}=\{\mathbf{s}_{i}\}\cup\{\mathbf{S}_{I}\}, where all 𝐬i,𝐒I∈[0,1]3\mathbf{s}_{i},\mathbf{S}_{I}\in[0,1]^{3}. The mapping from fractional to real coordinates is given by 𝒳=L⊤​𝒮\mathcal{X}=L^{\top}\mathcal{S}, where LL is the lattice matrix and L⊤​𝒮=(L⊤​s1,…,L⊤​sN,L⊤​S1,…,L⊤​SN)L^{\top}\mathcal{S}=(L^{\top}s_{1},\ldots,L^{\top}s_{N},L^{\top}S_{1},\ldots,L^{\top}S_{N}). Defining g=L​L⊤g=LL^{\top} and g−1=(L−1)⊤​L−1g^{-1}=(L^{-1})^{\top}L^{-1}, the local estimator becomes,

Gloc​(𝒮)\displaystyle G_{\text{loc}}(\mathcal{S}) =Kloc​(𝒮)+Vloc​(𝒮)\displaystyle=K_{\text{loc}}(\mathcal{S})+V_{\text{loc}}(\mathcal{S}) (S3)
Kloc​(𝒮)\displaystyle K_{\text{loc}}(\mathcal{S}) =−∑p12​mp[∑α,βg−1α,β∂2∂spα∂spβlnΨ(𝒮)\displaystyle=-\sum_{p}\frac{1}{2m_{p}}[\sum_{\alpha,\beta}g^{-1}_{\alpha,\beta}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial_{s_{p}}^{\alpha}\partial_{s_{p}}^{\beta}}\ln\Psi(\mathcal{S})
+(L−1∇splnΨ(𝒮))2]\displaystyle+(L^{-1}\nabla_{s_{p}}\ln\Psi(\mathcal{S}))^{2}]
Vloc​(𝒮)\displaystyle V_{\text{loc}}(\mathcal{S}) =V⁡(L⊤​𝒮)+P​Ω=V⁡(L⊤​𝒮)+P​detL\displaystyle=V(L^{\top}\mathcal{S})+P\Omega=V(L^{\top}\mathcal{S})+P\det L

where mp={1,p≤NM,N<p≤2​Nm_{p}=\begin{cases}1,&p\leq N\\ M,&N<p\leq 2N\end{cases}. The lattice is characterized by six parameters (a,b,c,α,β,γ)(a,b,c,\alpha,\beta,\gamma), with a,b,ca,b,c the lengths of the three basis vectors and α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma the angles between them. The lattice matrix LL is written as

L=(a00b​cos⁡γb​sin⁡γ0c​cos⁡β−csinβcosα∗csinβsinα∗),cos⁡α∗=cos⁡β​cos⁡γ−cos⁡αsin⁡β​sin⁡γ.L=\begin{pmatrix}a&0&0\\ b\cos\gamma&b\sin\gamma&0\\ c\cos\beta&-c\sin\beta\cos\alpha^{*}&c\sin\beta\sin\alpha^{*}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\cos\alpha^{*}=\frac{\cos\beta\cos\gamma-\cos\alpha}{\sin\beta\sin\gamma}. (S4)

For clarity, we assume the wavefunction in the NVT ensemble has the form Ψθ∪Lfixed​(𝒳)NVT\Psi_{\theta\cup L_{\text{fixed}}}(\mathcal{X})_{\text{NVT}}. The NPT wavefunction is defined via the NVT form in the unit cube,

Ψθ​(𝒮)NPT≡Ψθ∪L=I​(𝒮)NVT.\Psi_{\theta}(\mathcal{S})_{\text{NPT}}\equiv\Psi_{\theta\cup L=I}(\mathcal{S})_{\text{NVT}}. (S5)

so that geometry enters only through the operator and coordinate map.

III Exact-factorization kinetic-energy diagnostic

We adopt the exact-factorization gauge [2, 50],

χEF​(𝐑)=[∫d​𝐫​|Ψ⁡(𝐫,𝐑)|2]1/2,Φ𝐑​(𝐫)=Ψ⁡(𝐫,𝐑)χEF​(𝐑),\chi_{\rm EF}(\mathbf{R})=\left[\int d\mathbf{r}\,|\Psi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R})|^{2}\right]^{1/2},\qquad\Phi_{\mathbf{R}}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{\Psi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R})}{\chi_{\rm EF}(\mathbf{R})}, (S6)

for which ∫d​𝐫​|Φ𝐑​(𝐫)|2=1\int d\mathbf{r}\,|\Phi_{\mathbf{R}}(\mathbf{r})|^{2}=1 at each 𝐑\mathbf{R}.

The gauge-covariant decomposition is

KBOEF\displaystyle K_{\rm BO}^{\rm EF} =12​M​∑I∫d​𝐑​|[−i​∇𝐑I+𝐀I​(𝐑)]​χEF​(𝐑)|2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2M}\sum_{I}\int d\mathbf{R}\,\left|[-i\nabla_{\mathbf{R}_{I}}+\mathbf{A}_{I}(\mathbf{R})]\chi_{\rm EF}(\mathbf{R})\right|^{2}, (S7)
Knon​-​BOEF\displaystyle K_{\rm non\mbox{-}BO}^{\rm EF} =12​M​∑I∫d​𝐑​|χEF​(𝐑)|2​[⟨∇𝐑IΦ𝐑​|∇𝐑IΦ𝐑⟩𝐫−|⟨Φ𝐑|​∇𝐑IΦ𝐑⟩𝐫|2],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2M}\sum_{I}\int d\mathbf{R}\,|\chi_{\rm EF}(\mathbf{R})|^{2}\left[\langle\nabla_{\mathbf{R}_{I}}\Phi_{\mathbf{R}}|\nabla_{\mathbf{R}_{I}}\Phi_{\mathbf{R}}\rangle_{\mathbf{r}}-|\langle\Phi_{\mathbf{R}}|\nabla_{\mathbf{R}_{I}}\Phi_{\mathbf{R}}\rangle_{\mathbf{r}}|^{2}\right], (S8)

where

𝐀I​(𝐑)=⟨Φ𝐑|−i​∇𝐑I|Φ𝐑⟩𝐫.\mathbf{A}_{I}(\mathbf{R})=\langle\Phi_{\mathbf{R}}|-i\nabla_{\mathbf{R}_{I}}|\Phi_{\mathbf{R}}\rangle_{\mathbf{r}}. (S9)

The second integrand is the squared norm of the component of ∇𝐑IΦ𝐑\nabla_{\mathbf{R}_{I}}\Phi_{\mathbf{R}} orthogonal to Φ𝐑\Phi_{\mathbf{R}}; it is non-negative and invariant under the remaining phase gauge.

We evaluate the fixed-𝐑\mathbf{R} electronic inner products by sampling nuclear snapshots from the optimized NNVMC distribution and then performing electron-only Metropolis sampling. Two independent calculations give EF-gauge kinetic-energy ratios of approximately 3.7%. The gauge-invariant total nuclear kinetic energy remains approximately 0.386 Ha. The EF ratio is stable when the numbers of nuclear snapshots and electron walkers are increased. It provides a robust measure of kinetic coupling inside the optimized full wave function; a direct energetic comparison can be obtained from a separate BO-constrained optimization.

IV Benchmark statistics and autocorrelation

The benchmark inference used B=1024B=1024 independent chains and M=10,000M=10{,}000 saved records per chain, with 50 Metropolis proposal steps between saved records. If EmiE_{m}^{i} is the local energy for record mm in chain ii, we define

Em=1B​∑i=1BEmi,σm2=1B​∑i=1B(Emi−Em)2.E_{m}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}E_{m}^{i},\qquad\sigma_{m}^{2}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}(E_{m}^{i}-E_{m})^{2}. (S10)

Table I of the main text reports the means of Em/NE_{m}/N and σm2/N\sigma_{m}^{2}/N over the saved-record index mm. The variance is the width of the local-energy distribution. For either saved-record series Xm=Em/NX_{m}=E_{m}/N or Xm=σm2/NX_{m}=\sigma_{m}^{2}/N, we define X¯=M−1​∑m=1MXm\overline{X}=M^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^{M}X_{m} and sX2=(M−1)−1​∑m=1M(Xm−X¯)2s_{X}^{2}=(M-1)^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^{M}(X_{m}-\overline{X})^{2}. The parenthesized uncertainties in Table I of the main text are Δuncorr​(X¯)=sX/M\Delta_{\rm uncorr}(\overline{X})=s_{X}/\sqrt{M} and do not include an autocorrelation correction.

Autocorrelation was evaluated along mm, not across the independent-chain index. For a saved-record series XmX_{m}, we use

gX=1+2​∑k=1KXρX​(k),Δcorr​(X¯)=sXM​gX.g_{X}=1+2\sum_{k=1}^{K_{X}}\rho_{X}(k),\qquad\Delta_{\rm corr}(\overline{X})=\frac{s_{X}}{\sqrt{M}}\sqrt{g_{X}}. (S11)

One unit of lag is one saved-record interval, or 50 proposal steps. For E/NE/N, KE=20K_{E}=20, τint,E≃0.82\tau_{\rm int,E}\simeq 0.82, gE≃1.64g_{E}\simeq 1.64, and Δcorr​(E/N)=6.9×10−6\Delta_{\rm corr}(E/N)=6.9\times 10^{-6} Ha/atom. For σ2/N\sigma^{2}/N, Kσ2=1K_{\sigma^{2}}=1, τint,σ2≃0.5\tau_{\rm int,\sigma^{2}}\simeq 0.5, gσ2≃1g_{\sigma^{2}}\simeq 1, and Δcorr​(σ2/N)=4.8×10−5\Delta_{\rm corr}(\sigma^{2}/N)=4.8\times 10^{-5} Ha2/atom.

V Training Parameters and Training Curves

Table S1 lists the hyperparameters for the benchmark calculation of a dynamic BCC lattice at rs=1.31r_{s}=1.31 in the NVT ensemble, while Table S2 details those for various initial structures in the broken symmetry phase under the NPT ensemble. For the NPT training, we adopted a multi-stage strategy comprising three parts: (1) Warmup, where lattice parameters are fixed and wavefunction parameters are optimized to establish a high-quality initial wavefunction; (2) Lattice training, where wavefunction parameters are frozen while lattice parameters are optimized; and (3) Wavefunction training, which mirrors the warmup phase but involves fewer steps. The overall protocol begins with the initial Warmup phase, followed by an alternating cycle of Lattice training and Wavefunction training.

To demonstrate that noise may be beneficial in the simulated annealing process, Fig. S1 compares the training curves of two distinct annealing strategies: (i) a low-noise scheme that averages 10 independent enthalpy estimates per step, and (ii) a high-noise scheme that uses a single estimate but allows for 10 times as many steps. By design, the total computational cost for enthalpy evaluation remains identical for both methods. The results indicate that while both strategies converge to approximately the same enthalpy, the high-noise strategy exhibits faster convergence and yields lower variance. This demonstrates that the statistical noise of the enthalpy estimator supplies an effective stochastic driving force that enhances barrier crossing and accelerates convergence.

In Fig. S2, the left panel displays the training curves for the BCC dynamic lattice at rs=1.31r_{s}=1.31 within the NVT ensemble. Here, we benchmark our approach against other VMC methods, including NQS and traditional DMC, the latter of which serves as the lowest-energy reference in traditional methods. The right panel illustrates the training curves for various initial structures at Pext=130P_{\text{ext}}=130 GPa within the NPT ensemble(P​21/cP2_{1}/c is first training at Pext=10P_{\text{ext}}=10 GPa, and then at 130 GPa). These results identify the C​m​c​mCmcm phase as the lowest-energy structure among the tested structures at this pressure. The final enthalpies based on inference with 10000 steps after training are summarized in Table S3. The structure with the lowest enthalpy is listed in Table S4. To assess finite size effects, we also performed twist averaged boundary conditions (TABC) [65] calculations with a 2×2×22\times 2\times 2 twist grid; the training curves are shown in Fig. S3 and the corresponding enthalpies are compared alongside the PBC results in Table S3.

In Fig. S4, we present the evolution of the lattice parameters and the volume per atom as a function of the training steps. For simplicity, the lattice angles were fixed at α=β=γ=90∘\alpha=\beta=\gamma=90^{\circ} in Eq. S4 throughout the training, and allowing them to relax produces no appreciable deviation from this constraint as shown in Fig. S5.

VI XRD analysis of candidate structures

Figure S6 displays the structures analyzed in the XRD patterns of Fig. 4 of the main text. The P​21/c​-​8P2_{1}/c\text{-}8 and P​21/c​-​24P2_{1}/c\text{-}24 phases were taken from Refs. [59] and [96], respectively, with all other structures taken from Ref. [97]. A DFT variable-cell relaxation was performed to obtain the structural parameters at 130 GPa.

For each candidate, the common scale factor is s=(Vexp/Vcalc)1/3s=(V_{\rm exp}/V_{\rm calc})^{1/3}, so that dh​k​lscaled=s​dh​k​lcalcd_{hkl}^{\rm scaled}=s\,d_{hkl}^{\rm calc}. We quantify the remaining peak-position differences with

Δsim→exp\displaystyle\Delta_{\rm sim\to exp} =[1Nsim​∑iminj⁡(disim−djexp)2]1/2,\displaystyle=\left[\frac{1}{N_{\rm sim}}\sum_{i}\min_{j}(d_{i}^{\rm sim}-d_{j}^{\rm exp})^{2}\right]^{1/2}, (S12)
Δexp→sim\displaystyle\Delta_{\rm exp\to sim} =[1Nexp​∑jmini⁡(djexp−disim)2]1/2.\displaystyle=\left[\frac{1}{N_{\rm exp}}\sum_{j}\min_{i}(d_{j}^{\rm exp}-d_{i}^{\rm sim})^{2}\right]^{1/2}. (S13)

These metrics provide a reproducible peak-position comparison complementary to a full-profile structural refinement; the results are summarized in Table S5.

To estimate coherent Bragg-intensity changes from the sampled nuclear density, we first remove global center-of-mass drift by aligning every |Ψ|2|\Psi|^{2} nuclear configuration to the static reference and wrapping it into the periodic cell. For reciprocal vector 𝐆α=2​π​L−T​𝐡α\mathbf{G}_{\alpha}=2\pi L^{-T}\mathbf{h}_{\alpha}, define

ρs​(𝐆)=∑j=1Natomei​𝐆⋅𝐫s,j,ρstatic​(𝐆)=∑jei​𝐆⋅𝐫jstatic.\rho_{s}(\mathbf{G})=\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\rm atom}}e^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{s,j}},\qquad\rho_{\rm static}(\mathbf{G})=\sum_{j}e^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{j}^{\rm static}}. (S14)

For peak group pp, with multiplicity mαm_{\alpha},

Spstatic\displaystyle S_{p}^{\rm static} =∑α∈pmα​|ρstatic​(𝐆α)|2,\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\in p}m_{\alpha}|\rho_{\rm static}(\mathbf{G}_{\alpha})|^{2}, (S15)
Spcoh\displaystyle S_{p}^{\rm coh} =∑α∈pmα​|⟨ρs​(𝐆α)⟩s|2,\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\in p}m_{\alpha}|\langle\rho_{s}(\mathbf{G}_{\alpha})\rangle_{s}|^{2}, (S16)

and the coherent correction is

Rpcoh=SpcohSpstatic,Ipcoh,corr=Ipstatic​Rpcoh.R_{p}^{\rm coh}=\frac{S_{p}^{\rm coh}}{S_{p}^{\rm static}},\qquad I_{p}^{\rm coh,corr}=I_{p}^{\rm static}R_{p}^{\rm coh}. (S17)

This construction retains the static peak positions and X-ray prefactors while incorporating the coherent Bragg-intensity correction. A full quantum diffraction treatment would additionally describe diffuse scattering and peak-position shifts. The correction suppresses the feature near the first experimental line and the weak features near 1.3 and 1.7 Å, while slightly enhancing the third feature. These intensity trends provide a qualitative view of quantum nuclear effects, with the third feature remaining weak.

VII Raman and IR analysis

This analysis uses the correlation method [89] to determine the vibrational properties of solid hydrogen. The isolated H2\mathrm{H}_{2} molecule belongs to the linear D∞​hD_{\infty h} point group. In the solid state, hydrogen crystallizes in the orthorhombic space group C​m​c​mCmcm, which corresponds to the factor group D2​hD_{2h}.The molecular centers of mass occupy three distinct Wyckoff positions: two 4​c4c sites and one 8​g8g site. The site symmetries for these molecular centers are C2​vC_{2v} for the 4​c4c positions and CsC_{s} for the 8​g8g positions. The derivation of the Raman and IR active modes proceeds by:

  1. 1.

    characterizing the modes of the isolated H2\mathrm{H}_{2} molecule;

  2. 2.

    constructing correlation tables linking D∞​hD_{\infty h} to the site symmetries C2​vC_{2v} and CsC_{s};

  3. 3.

    correlating these site symmetries with the factor group D2​hD_{2h}; and

  4. 4.

    deriving the selection rules for the crystal lattice.

VII.1 Mode of Hydrogen Molecule H2\mathrm{H}_{2}

A diatomic molecule possesses 6 degrees of freedom (dof):

  1. 1.

    Translations (3 dof): Basis functions x,y,zx,y,z, corresponding to Πu​(x,y)\Pi_{u}(x,y) and Σu+​(z)\Sigma_{u}^{+}(z) representations.

  2. 2.

    Rotations (2 dof): Basis functions Rx,RyR_{x},R_{y}, transforming as Πg​(Rx,Ry)\Pi_{g}(R_{x},R_{y}).

  3. 3.

    Vibration (1 dof): The vibrational mode transforms as Σg+\Sigma_{g}^{+}.

VII.2 Correlation table for D∞​hD_{\infty h} to site symmetry C2​vC_{2v} and CsC_{s}

We first restrict the representation in D∞​hD_{\infty h} into site symmetries C2​vC_{2v} and CsC_{s}, it can be established from standard correlation relation table.

  1. 1.

    D∞​h→C2​vD_{\infty h}\rightarrow C_{2v}:

    1. (a)

      Σg+→Ag→A1\Sigma_{g}^{+}\to A_{g}\to A_{1}

    2. (b)

      Πg→B2​g+B3​g→A2+B1\Pi_{g}\to B_{2g}+B_{3g}\to A_{2}+B_{1}

    3. (c)

      Πu→B2​u+B3​u→A1+B2\Pi_{u}\to B_{2u}+B_{3u}\to A_{1}+B_{2}

    4. (d)

      Σu+→B1​u→B1\Sigma_{u}^{+}\to B_{1u}\to B_{1}

  2. 2.

    D∞​h→CsD_{\infty h}\rightarrow C_{s}:

    1. (a)

      Σg+→Ag→A′\Sigma_{g}^{+}\to A_{g}\to A^{{}^{\prime}}

    2. (b)

      Πg→B2​g+B3​g→2A′′\Pi_{g}\to B_{2g}+B_{3g}\to 2A^{{}^{\prime\prime}}

    3. (c)

      Πu→B2​u+B3​u→2A′\Pi_{u}\to B_{2u}+B_{3u}\to 2A^{{}^{\prime}}

    4. (d)

      Σu+→B1​u→A′′\Sigma_{u}^{+}\to B_{1u}\to A^{{}^{\prime\prime}}

VII.3 Induced Representations in the Factor Group D2​hD_{2h}

To determine the representations induced from the subgroups C2​vC_{2v} and CsC_{s} into the factor group D2​hD_{2h}, we employ Frobenius reciprocity. This principle states that the multiplicity of an irreducible representation ρ\rho of a group GG in the induced representation of a subgroup HH is equal to the multiplicity of the representation of HH in the restriction of ρ\rho to HH, ⟨IndHG​(σ),ρ⟩G=⟨σ,ResH​(ρ)⟩H\langle\mathrm{Ind}_{H}^{G}(\sigma),\,\rho\rangle_{G}=\langle\sigma,\,\mathrm{Res}_{H}(\rho)\rangle_{H}. Consequently, the standard correlation tables from D2​hD_{2h} down to C2​vC_{2v} and CsC_{s} allow us to determine the induced modes.

  1. 1.

    C2​v→D2​hC_{2v}\rightarrow D_{2h}:

    1. (a)

      A1→Ag+B2​uA_{1}\to A_{g}+B_{2u}

    2. (b)

      A2→Au+B2​gA_{2}\to A_{u}+B_{2g}

    3. (c)

      B1→B3​g+B1​uB_{1}\to B_{3g}+B_{1u}

    4. (d)

      B2→B1​g+B3​uB_{2}\to B_{1g}+B_{3u}

  2. 2.

    Cs→D2​hC_{s}\rightarrow D_{2h}:

    1. (a)

      A′→Ag+B1​g+B2​u+B3​uA^{{}^{\prime}}\to A_{g}+B_{1g}+B_{2u}+B_{3u}

    2. (b)

      A′′→Au+B1​u+B2​g+B3​gA^{{}^{\prime\prime}}\to A_{u}+B_{1u}+B_{2g}+B_{3g}

VII.4 Raman and IR Active Modes of Solid Hydrogen

Thus, for the vibron:

  1. 1.

    site A(4​c4c): Σg+→Ag→A1→Ag+B2​u\Sigma_{g}^{+}\to A_{g}\to A_{1}\to A_{g}+B_{2u}

  2. 2.

    site B(4​c4c): Σg+→Ag→A1→Ag+B2​u\Sigma_{g}^{+}\to A_{g}\to A_{1}\to A_{g}+B_{2u}

  3. 3.

    site C(8​g8g): Σg+→Ag→A′→Ag+B1​g+B2​u+B3​u\Sigma_{g}^{+}\to A_{g}\to A^{{}^{\prime}}\to A_{g}+B_{1g}+B_{2u}+B_{3u}

Thus, the representation of the vibron is

Γv​i​b​r​o​n=2​(Ag+B2​u)+(Ag+B1​g+B2​u+B3​u)=3​Ag+3​B2​u+B1​g+B3​u\Gamma_{vibron}=2(A_{g}+B_{2u})+(A_{g}+B_{1g}+B_{2u}+B_{3u})=3A_{g}+3B_{2u}+B_{1g}+B_{3u} (S18)

For the Libron(phonon):

  1. 1.

    site A(4​c4c): Πg→B2​g+B3​g→A2+B1→Au+B2​g+B3​g+B1​u\Pi_{g}\to B_{2g}+B_{3g}\to A_{2}+B_{1}\to A_{u}+B_{2g}+B_{3g}+B_{1u}

  2. 2.

    site B(4​c4c): Πg→B2​g+B3​g→A2+B1→Au+B2​g+B3​g+B1​u\Pi_{g}\to B_{2g}+B_{3g}\to A_{2}+B_{1}\to A_{u}+B_{2g}+B_{3g}+B_{1u}

  3. 3.

    site C(8​g8g): Πg→B2​g+B3​g→2A′′→2Au+2B1​u+2B2​g+2B3​g\Pi_{g}\to B_{2g}+B_{3g}\to 2A^{{}^{\prime\prime}}\to 2A_{u}+2B_{1u}+2B_{2g}+2B_{3g}

Thus, the representation of the libron is

Γl​i​b​r​o​n\displaystyle\Gamma_{libron} =2​(Au+B2​g+B3​g+B1​u)+2​Au+2​B1​u+2​B2​g+2​B3​g\displaystyle=2(A_{u}+B_{2g}+B_{3g}+B_{1u})+2A_{u}+2B_{1u}+2B_{2g}+2B_{3g} (S19)
=4​Au+4​B1​u+4​B2​g+4​B3​g\displaystyle=4A_{u}+4B_{1u}+4B_{2g}+4B_{3g}

Translational Phonons

  1. 1.

    site A(4​c4c): Σu++Πu→B1​u+B2​u+B3​u→A1+B1+B2→Ag+B2​u+B3​g+B1​u+B1​g+B3​u\Sigma_{u}^{+}+\Pi_{u}\to B_{1u}+B_{2u}+B_{3u}\to A_{1}+B_{1}+B_{2}\to A_{g}+B_{2u}+B_{3g}+B_{1u}+B_{1g}+B_{3u}

  2. 2.

    site B(4​c4c): Σu++Πu→B1​u+B2​u+B3​u→A1+B1+B2→Ag+B2​u+B3​g+B1​u+B1​g+B3​u\Sigma_{u}^{+}+\Pi_{u}\to B_{1u}+B_{2u}+B_{3u}\to A_{1}+B_{1}+B_{2}\to A_{g}+B_{2u}+B_{3g}+B_{1u}+B_{1g}+B_{3u}

  3. 3.

    site C(8​g8g): Σu++Πu→B1​u+B2​u+B3​u→2A′+A′′→Au+B1​u+B2​g+B3​g+2Ag+2B1​g+2B2​u+2B3​u\Sigma_{u}^{+}+\Pi_{u}\to B_{1u}+B_{2u}+B_{3u}\to 2A^{{}^{\prime}}+A^{{}^{\prime\prime}}\to A_{u}+B_{1u}+B_{2g}+B_{3g}+2A_{g}+2B_{1g}+2B_{2u}+2B_{3u}

Summing over all sites yields:

Γt​r​a​n​s\displaystyle\Gamma_{trans} =2​Ag+2​B2​u+2​B3​g+2​B1​u+2​B1​g+2​B3​u\displaystyle=2A_{g}+2B_{2u}+2B_{3g}+2B_{1u}+2B_{1g}+2B_{3u} (S20)
+Au+B1​u+B2​g+B3​g+2​Ag+2​B1​g+2​B2​u+2​B3​u\displaystyle+A_{u}+B_{1u}+B_{2g}+B_{3g}+2A_{g}+2B_{1g}+2B_{2u}+2B_{3u}
=Au+4​B1​g+4​B2​u+3​B3​g+4​Ag+B2​g+3​B1​u+4​B3​u\displaystyle=A_{u}+4B_{1g}+4B_{2u}+3B_{3g}+4A_{g}+B_{2g}+3B_{1u}+4B_{3u}

Subtracting the acoustic branches (B1​u+B2​u+B3​uB_{1u}+B_{2u}+B_{3u}):

Γo​p​t​i​c​a​l\displaystyle\Gamma_{optical} =Γt​r​a​n​s−Γa​c​o​u​s​t​i​c\displaystyle=\Gamma_{trans}-\Gamma_{acoustic} (S21)
=Au+4​B1​g+3​B2​u+3​B3​g+4​Ag+B2​g+2​B1​u+3​B3​u\displaystyle=A_{u}+4B_{1g}+3B_{2u}+3B_{3g}+4A_{g}+B_{2g}+2B_{1u}+3B_{3u}

The optical phonon is

Γo​p​t​p​h​o=Γo​p​t​i​c​a​l+Γl​i​b​r​o​n=5​Au+4​B1​g+3​B2​u+7​B3​g+4​Ag+5​B2​g+6​B1​u+3​B3​u\Gamma_{optpho}=\Gamma_{optical}+\Gamma_{libron}=5A_{u}+4B_{1g}+3B_{2u}+7B_{3g}+4A_{g}+5B_{2g}+6B_{1u}+3B_{3u} (S22)

Note that AuA_{u} modes are silent (inactive in both Raman and IR). In summary, the Raman and IR active modes are:

ΓRamanvibron\displaystyle\Gamma_{\mathrm{Raman}}^{\mathrm{vibron}} =3​Ag+B1​g,\displaystyle=3A_{g}+B_{1g}, (S23)
ΓIRvibron\displaystyle\Gamma_{\mathrm{IR}}^{\mathrm{vibron}} =3​B2​u+B3​u,\displaystyle=3B_{2u}+B_{3u}, (S24)
ΓRamanphonon\displaystyle\Gamma_{\mathrm{Raman}}^{\mathrm{phonon}} =4​B1​g+7​B3​g+4​Ag+5​B2​g,\displaystyle=4B_{1g}+7B_{3g}+4A_{g}+5B_{2g}, (S25)
ΓIRphonon\displaystyle\Gamma_{\mathrm{IR}}^{\mathrm{phonon}} =3​B2​u+6​B1​u+3​B3​u.\displaystyle=3B_{2u}+6B_{1u}+3B_{3u}. (S26)

These correlation tables establish the symmetry-allowed modes. Comparison with the observed subset therefore provides a symmetry-level compatibility check, while frequencies and intensities remain targets for future calculations.
